questions.stem: Identify the error and choose the improved sentence: 'She is more smarter than her sister.'

options.option_text: She is more smarter than her sister.
She is smarter than her sister.
She is the smartest than her sister.
She is most smart than her sister.

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'More smarter' is a double comparative — both 'more' and '-er' convey comparison simultaneously, which is redundant and grammatically wrong. Rule: use EITHER '-er' suffix (smarter) OR 'more' + adjective (more intelligent) — never both together.

questions.stem: Improve the sentence: 'The committee have decided to postpone the meeting.'

options.option_text: The committee have decided to postpone the meeting.
The committee has decided to postpone the meeting.
The committee decided in postponing the meeting.
The committee are deciding to postpone the meeting.

questions.explanation: B is correct. In formal Indian-English (as per SSC/Bank exam standards), collective nouns (committee, team, jury, class) take singular verbs: 'The committee has decided.' British English allows plural agreement, but exam questions follow the singular rule. 'Decided to' (not 'in') is the correct infinitive construction.

questions.stem: Choose the correct improvement for: 'He told that he would come tomorrow.'

options.option_text: He told that he would come tomorrow.
He said that he would come the next day.
He told that he will come tomorrow.
He said that he will come tomorrow.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Two errors: (1) 'told' requires an object ('told me/him/them' — told WHOM); 'said' can be used without an object before 'that'. (2) In reported speech, direct 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'. Corrected: 'He said that he would come the next day.' Rule: tell + object + that; say + that (no object).

questions.stem: Improve the sentence: 'He is working in this company since five years.'

options.option_text: He is working in this company since five years.
He has been working in this company for five years.
He worked in this company for five years.
He is working in this company for five years.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Two errors: (1) Tense should be present perfect continuous (has been working) for an action that started in the past and continues now. (2) 'since five years' is wrong — 'since' = specific point in time; 'for' = duration. → 'He has been working in this company for five years.'

questions.stem: Choose the correct version: 'One of the boy has to stay back.'

options.option_text: One of the boy has to stay back.
One of the boys have to stay back.
One of the boys has to stay back.
One of the boys have stayed back.

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'One of the boys' — the subject is 'ONE' (singular), so the verb must be singular ('has'). The phrase 'of the boys' is a prepositional phrase that does NOT affect verb agreement. Rule: 'One of the + plural noun + singular verb.' This is a very common error in competitive exams.

questions.stem: Improve: 'He is too weak that he cannot walk.'

options.option_text: He is too weak that he cannot walk.
He is so weak that he cannot walk.
He is too weak for walk.
He is too weak for him to walk.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Two valid structures: (1) 'so...that' = 'He is so weak that he cannot walk.' (2) 'too...to' = 'He is too weak to walk.' The original 'too...that' is non-standard and wrong. Never say 'too + adj + that' — use 'so + adj + that' OR 'too + adj + to + verb'.

questions.stem: Find the error: 'Hardly had he reached the station when the train left.'

options.option_text: Replace 'when' with 'than'
The sentence is correct as it is.
Replace 'Hardly had' with 'As soon as he had'
Replace 'when' with 'before'

questions.explanation: B is correct. The sentence 'Hardly had he reached the station when the train left' is grammatically correct. Pattern: Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + V3 + WHEN + subject + past simple. 'No sooner + had + subject + V3 + THAN' (uses 'than', not 'when'). The distinction: 'hardly/scarcely' → 'when'; 'no sooner' → 'than'.

questions.stem: Improve: 'Each of the students are required to submit their assignment.'

options.option_text: Each of the students are required to submit their assignment.
Each of the students is required to submit their assignment.
Each of the students are required to submit his assignment.
All of the students is required to submit their assignment.

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Each' is always singular — verb must be 'is'. 'Each of the students IS'. 'Their' as a gender-neutral singular pronoun is now widely accepted even in formal writing. Compare: 'Each' → is; 'Every' → is; 'Either/Neither' → is; 'All/Both' → are.

questions.stem: Improve the sentence: 'The police have arrested many a thief.'

options.option_text: The police have arrested many a thief.
The police has arrested many thieves.
The police have arrested many thieves.
The police have arrested many a thieves.

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Many a + singular noun' is an idiomatic expression meaning 'many'. 'Many a thief' = many thieves (but uses singular noun). The verb agrees with the main subject: 'police' (always plural) → 'have'. The original sentence is correct. Note: 'police' is always plural in English (never 'polices').

options.option_text: She is junior than me.
She is more junior than me.
She is junior to me.
She is the most junior than me.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Latin-derived adjectives ending in -or (junior, senior, superior, inferior, prior, major, minor) already contain the comparative sense — they use 'to' instead of 'than', and never take 'more/most'. Always: 'senior to', 'inferior to', 'superior to', 'junior to'. Never: 'more senior than', 'senior than'.
